title: Fan out on a virtual thread per task

blocks.text: With virtual threads a blocking task no longer needs a pooled thread: the page's advice is one new virtual thread per task, from `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` in a `try`-with-resources block, whose `close()` waits for every task. A fixed pool of virtual threads is the pitfall to avoid: it caps how many tasks run at once, exactly like a pool of platform threads.

items: It calls `fetch` once per key, each call on its **own virtual thread**, and all the calls run **at the same time** (no cap on how many).
It returns the results in key order, after every call has finished.

blocks.text: The tests see that each call runs on a virtual thread and that every call is in flight at once; whether a thread is ever reused for a later call is not something they can force, so use the page's executor anyway.

items: If a call throws, `fetchAll` throws an `ExecutionException` whose cause is that exception.

rows: each call waits until all 1000 have started

cases.says: fetchAll returns one result per key, in key order.
A thousand fetches that each wait for all the others still finish: every fetch runs at the same time.
Each fetch runs on its own virtual thread.
When a fetch throws, fetchAll throws an ExecutionException caused by it.
2500 calls are all in flight at once: no pool size caps them, however large.

concepts: Virtual threads are daemon threads, so work started on them must be waited for or the program may end first.
Virtual threads are not pooled: a fixed pool of them caps concurrency exactly like a pool of platform threads.
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a new virtual thread for every task, and closing it in try-with-resources waits for all of them.
